description: Writing procedures and functions in Python, using local variables, and finding program errors.
content_html:
Why Break Code into Subprograms?

As programs grow longer, keeping everything in one flat block of code becomes unmanageable. A subprogram is a named block of code that does one clearly defined job. You call it by name whenever that job needs doing, rather than copying the code every time. Python supports two types of subprogram: procedures and functions. Edexcel is precise about the distinction — confusing them is one of the most penalised errors in exam answers.

Key Fact

A function MUST return a value using return. A procedure does NOT return a value. Both may take parameters. Writing “a function performs a task” without mentioning the return value is an incomplete definition that loses marks.

Procedures in Python

A procedure is defined with def, may take parameters, performs its task, and then simply ends. It does not hand anything back to the line that called it.

def print_greeting(name):
    print("Hello,", name, "- welcome to the system!")

# Calling the procedure
print_greeting("Priya")
print_greeting("Ali")

The procedure executes, produces output, and exits. The calling code receives nothing back. Good uses for procedures: printing a menu, displaying a result, writing a line to a file, sending a notification.

Functions in Python

A function is also defined with def, but it uses return to send a result back. The returned value replaces the function call in the expression where it appears.

def calculate_area(length, width):
    area = length * width
    return area

# Calling the function and using the returned value
room_area = calculate_area(5, 4)
print("Area:", room_area, "square metres")

# The return value can also be used directly in an expression:
if calculate_area(3, 3) > 8:
    print("Room is large enough")

A function that checks if a student has passed (score ≥ 50) and returns a Boolean:

def has_passed(score):
    if score >= 50:
        return True
    else:
        return False

result = has_passed(72)
print(result)    # True

result2 = has_passed(40)
print(result2)   # False

Predict the output: 72 ≥ 50 so the first call returns True. 40 < 50 so the second returns False. The function’s return value is captured in a variable and then printed. This predict-before-run habit is essential for trace table questions.

Parameters

Parameters are the input variables listed in the subprogram’s definition. When you call the subprogram, you pass arguments — the actual values — which are assigned to the parameter names. The order must match: the first argument goes to the first parameter, and so on.

def greet_student(first_name, year_group):
    print("Welcome, Year", year_group, "student", first_name)

greet_student("Beth", 10)   # first_name = "Beth", year_group = 10

Local and Global Variables — Scope

Scope describes which parts of a program can read or change a variable. A local variable is declared inside a def block. It is created when the function is called and destroyed when it returns. Nothing outside the function can access it.

def calculate_tax(price):
    tax_rate = 0.20    # local variable
    tax = price * tax_rate
    return tax

# tax_rate and tax do NOT exist out here
print(calculate_tax(100))   # 20.0

A global variable is declared at module level (outside all functions). It can be read anywhere in the program. To reassign it inside a function, you must use the global keyword; otherwise Python creates a new local variable with the same name instead.

Local variables reduce the risk of bugs. If a global variable called score is shared across ten functions, any one of them could accidentally overwrite it. A bug that corrupts the score could be anywhere in the program — finding it means checking all ten functions. If score is instead a local parameter, only that function can change it. The problem is isolated immediately.

Use global variables only for values that genuinely need to be shared across the whole program — for example, a configuration setting loaded once at start-up, or a game’s running total score that every function needs to update.

Built-in and Library Subprograms

Python comes with many built-in subprograms that are always available: print(), input(), len(), int(), float(), str(), range(). These are functions — most of them return a value. Python also has an extensive standard library of library subprograms that must be imported before use, such as import math and then math.sqrt(25).

Types of Program Error

When a program fails, the error falls into one of three categories. Understanding which type of error you are dealing with determines where to look for the fix.

A syntax error occurs when the code violates the rules of Python. The program will not run at all. Python reports the line number and type of problem. Common causes: missing colon at the end of an if or def line, misspelled keyword, unmatched brackets.

A runtime error occurs during execution. The syntax is correct, so Python starts running the program — but something goes wrong mid-execution. Examples: dividing by zero (ZeroDivisionError), using an index beyond the end of a list (IndexError), trying to convert “hello” to an integer (ValueError).

A logic error is the most difficult to find. The program runs without crashing — but it produces the wrong answer. Examples: using > when the condition should be >=, updating a total inside a loop but printing it inside the loop instead of after it, or initialising an accumulator to 1 instead of 0.

Key Fact

Syntax error: program won’t run at all — Python language rules broken. Runtime error: program starts but crashes during execution — impossible operation attempted. Logic error: program runs to completion but produces the wrong output — the algorithm itself is flawed. Only a logic error can be invisible to Python — the other two produce explicit error messages.

Test Data — Normal, Boundary and Erroneous

Testing requires choosing test data that exercises different parts of the program. Three categories of test data cover the essential cases for any input that must lie within a range.

Normal test data uses typical values well within the valid range. For an age input (0 to 120), normal data might be 25, 45, 67. Boundary test data (also called edge data) tests the extreme limits: for the range 0–120, test 0, 1, 119, and 120. Erroneous test data is deliberately invalid: -1, 121, or “hello” for an age field.

Trace the output of the following function for the call classify(73):

def classify(score):
    if score >= 80:
        return "Distinction"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "Merit"
    else:
        return "Pass"

result = classify(73)
print(result)

Trace: score = 73. Is 73 ≥ 80? No. Is 73 ≥ 60? Yes → return “Merit”. result = “Merit”. Output: Merit. When tracing a function, substitute the argument value for the parameter name and follow each condition in order.
exam_tip_html: The most common mark loss in “Write a Subprogram” questions is a function that forgets to include return, or a procedure that accidentally returns a value. Always write the signature first (def name(parameters):), then the body, then return at the end if it is a function. For error-type questions, be precise: a syntax error means Python language rules are broken; a logic error means the algorithm produces wrong results but runs without crashing. “A mistake in the code” is too vague for marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A function MUST return a value using return. A procedure does NOT return a value. Both are defined with def and may take parameters.
  • Local variables exist only inside the subprogram where they are defined; global variables are accessible everywhere. Prefer local variables to reduce bugs and improve maintainability.
  • Three error types: syntax (code breaks Python rules, won't run), runtime (crashes during execution), logic (runs but produces wrong results). Test with normal, boundary and erroneous data.

practice_questions.text: Define the difference between a function and a procedure in Python.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A function returns a value to the calling code using return (1); a procedure performs a task but does not return a value (1).
Secure: One part correctly defined.
Developing: States both are defined with def without identifying the return-value distinction.
Emerging: Uses the terms interchangeably.

practice_questions.text:
Identify the type of error in each of the following:
(a) A program calculates the total of a list but initialises the total to 1 instead of 0, giving a result that is one too high.
(b) A program crashes when the user enters 'quit' into a field that expects an integer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) Logic error (1) — the program runs but produces the wrong result due to a flawed algorithm; (b) Runtime error (1) — int('quit') raises a ValueError during execution.
Secure: Both identified with imprecise explanation.
Developing: One correct identification.
Emerging: Both wrong or terms confused.

practice_questions.text:
Complete a trace table for the following Python code. Show the values of n and result for each call.
def double_it(n):
    result = n * 2
    return result

print(double_it(5))
print(double_it(12))
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Call 1: n=5, result=10, output 10 (1 per correct detail); Call 2: n=12, result=24, output 24 (1 per correct detail). 4 marks for all four values correct.
Secure: Three values correct.
Developing: Two values correct.
Emerging: Does not trace parameter substitution.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using local variables rather than global variables in a Python subprogram.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Local variables can only be accessed within their subprogram (1) so they cannot be accidentally changed by other parts of the program (1); this makes bugs easier to locate (1) because if the variable has the wrong value, only that subprogram can be responsible (1).
Secure: Correct advantage with partial explanation.
Developing: States local variables are inside the function without explaining the benefit.
Emerging: Confuses local and global scope.

practice_questions.text: Write a Python function called is_valid_age that takes an integer parameter age and returns True if the age is between 0 and 120 inclusive, and False otherwise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: def with correct function name and parameter (1); if condition checking age >= 0 and age <= 120 (1); return True in the valid branch (1); return False in the invalid branch (1); function called correctly with a test value (1); meaningful identifier names used (1).
Secure: Correct logic with one structural error.
Developing: Condition present but return values missing or wrong.
Emerging: No return statement used.

practice_questions.text: A programmer is testing a function that only accepts scores from 0 to 100. Describe the normal, boundary and erroneous test data they should use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Normal — typical values well within range, e.g. 50, 75 (1); explanation that normal data should produce correct expected output (1); boundary — values at the exact edges: 0, 1, 99, 100 (1); explanation that boundary tests verify edge conditions are handled correctly (1); erroneous — values outside the valid range or wrong type: -1, 101, 'hello' (1); explanation that erroneous data verifies the program handles invalid input gracefully (1).
Secure: All three types named with partial explanation.
Developing: Two types described.
Emerging: One type or no clear distinction between categories.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes a function in Python?
options: A block of code that performs a task and displays output
A block of code that performs a task and returns a value
A block of code with no parameters
A block of code that can only be called once

knowledge_checks.q: A program runs without crashing but outputs the wrong answer. What type of error is this?
A variable declared inside a Python function is called a _____ variable.
Test data that uses values at the exact edges of the valid input range is called _____ test data.
Match each error type to its description.
right: Program runs but produces wrong results
Program won't run — language rules broken

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between a function and a procedure in Python?
flashcard_questions.a: A function returns a value using return; a procedure does not.
The code breaks the rules of the Python language and the program cannot run.
While the program is executing — the syntax is valid but an impossible operation is attempted.
The program runs without crashing but produces incorrect results due to a flaw in the algorithm.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the return statement do in a Python function?
flashcard_questions.a: Sends a value back to the calling code and exits the function.

flashcard_questions.q: Where does a local variable exist in Python?
flashcard_questions.a: Inside the subprogram (def block) where it was declared — it cannot be accessed outside.

flashcard_questions.q: Give three examples of Python built-in subprograms.
flashcard_questions.a: Any three of: print(), input(), len(), int(), float(), str(), range().
Data at the exact edges of the valid input range, e.g. 0 and 100 for a 0–100 range.
Data clearly outside the valid range or of the wrong type, used to test invalid-input handling.

flashcard_questions.q: What kind of variable is accessible from any function in a Python program?
What Python keyword is used to define both functions and procedures?

glossary_terms.definition: A named, self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called by name from anywhere in the program.
A subprogram that performs a task but does not return a value to the calling code.
A subprogram that performs a task and returns a value to the calling code using the return statement.
Variables listed in a subprogram definition that receive values when the subprogram is called; the passed values are available inside the subprogram for the duration of the call.
The part of a program where a variable can be accessed; a variable's scope is determined by where it is declared.
A variable declared inside a subprogram that only exists while the subprogram is running and cannot be accessed from code outside it.
A variable declared outside all subprograms, accessible from any part of the program.
Subprograms provided as part of the Python language itself, available without importing anything, such as print(), input(), len() and int().
Subprograms provided in a Python module that must be imported before use, such as functions from the math or random modules.
An error caused by code that breaks the rules of the Python language, preventing the program from running at all.
An error that occurs while a program is running, causing it to crash; the code is syntactically valid but attempts an impossible operation.
An error where the program runs without crashing but produces incorrect results because the logic of the algorithm is flawed.
Test data that represents typical, expected values that the program should process correctly.
Test data that uses values at the exact edges of the valid range, to verify the boundary conditions of the program are handled correctly.
Test data that is clearly outside the valid range or of the wrong type, used to verify the program handles invalid input gracefully.
